Plus, investors await inflation data
 

You probably don’t need the government to tell you that the cost of living is up, but this morning’s consumer-price index reading will tell you how much prices officially rose in September. A hot CPI number could reverse a recent easing of bond yields from multidecade highs and pile pressure on the Fed for swifter action. A cool one would be celebrated. Thanks for the sentiment

 

Huh? According to one contrarian gauge, now might be a better time to scoop up stocks than the Covid panic, the height of the financial crisis, the aftermath of 9/11 attacks or the late 1970s energy crisis.

 

The granddaddy of all sentiment indicators, the University of Michigan’s long-running consumer survey, is often portrayed in headlines as a flashing red light for investors when it’s unusually low or a green light when it’s exuberant.

 

Extreme readings have almost always meant the opposite, though. Historic lows were hit in April 1980, Oct. 1990 and Nov. 2008—all buying opportunities. And the survey’s peak was in Jan. 2000, a great time to take profits in highflying tech stocks.

 

Lately, though, the results have shown a strict red-blue divide as the economic mood of Republicans or Democrats flipped with the occupant of The White House. That makes the headline number all but useless to investors. Last week’s preliminary October reading would be the second worst ever, and May’s was the lowest.

 

Luckily, asking professional investors how they feel and what they own still seems to work. Bank of America’s Global Fund Manager Survey, released this week, offers a treasure trove of detail.

 

Like the Michigan survey used to, BofA’s most reliable signals flash when too many respondents seem to be in agreement. The latest monthly edition, released on Tuesday by Chief Investment Strategist Michael Hartnett and his team, seems like one of those.

 

The percentage of respondents expecting “boom” conditions—above trend growth and inflation—was the highest since Feb. 2022, the starting point for the last bear market. Federal Reserve rate hikes that began the following month hit technology stocks especially hard.

 

Fund managers aren’t worried about that hot sector at the moment: Respondents were the most net overweight tech stocks since the summer of 2020, the height of the feverish post-Covid market rebound. They were last heavily underweight tech four years ago, just in time for ChatGPT’s release to supercharge the current AI-themed bull market.

 

Not all stocks are loved. Managers are most pessimistic about consumer discretionary stocks, with sentiment back to the depth of the 2008 recession.

 

Hartnett doesn’t just collect the data, he parses it, and his instinct is to go against the current. One rule he has is to recommend selling global equities when fund managers’ average cash levels drop below 5%. They’re now at 3.9%.

 

He offers the same recommendation when BofA’s Bull & Bear Indicator, a composite measure, rises above 5. It’s now at 5.1.

 

There’s one ray of sunshine in the survey. Fund managers’ biggest worries over the years—the 2013 “fiscal cliff,” a 2016 hard landing in China, Covid, EU disintegration, and a global recession following President Trump’s tariff onslaught—have regularly vanished from the headlines soon after.

 

Managers’ latest top fear is a disorderly rise in bond yields.

↘️Saudi Arabian Oil Co.: An office building at the Saudi state oil giant’s headquarters was struck yesterday by Yemen’s Houthi militants, as fighting intensified between the kingdom and the Iran-backed group. Shares of Aramco, as it is more commonly known, fell 1% in Riyadh.
